# SDNY Epstein Investigation **Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.* Edition label: `2026-11` > Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Jurisdiction:** Southern District of New York[^1] **Lead:** U.S. Attorney Geoff Berman[^2] **Key actions:** Epstein indictment (July 2019)[^3]; Maxwell indictment (June 2020)[^4]; Maxwell conviction (2021)[^5]

## Overview

Barr recalled Justice Department discussions about making sure the 2019 charges did not run afoul of the NPA.[^6]

## AG Barr's Role William Barr testified that he did not delve into the Epstein investigation and left it to the investigators:[^7] - Does not recall reviewing the indictment; may have been shown it[^8] - Did not approve charge decisions; does not recall approving subpoenas, though notes it's possible issues came up[^9] - Did not recall communicating directly with any SDNY line prosecutors[^10] - Barr recalled David Bowdich (FBI Deputy Director) as his primary FBI contact; Barr said he thought SDNY communications would have gone more to the Deputy Attorney General's office[^11] - Believed he was told the substance of Maxwell's case when prosecutors were ready to indict, but did not review the evidence himself[^12] Barr first learned of the investigation around the time of Epstein's arrest (July 2019), possibly slightly before.[^13]

## Investigation Scope (Barr's Account) Barr states he was never briefed that SDNY had actionable evidence against any of the prominently named figures:[^14] - Trump, Clinton, Richardson, Mitchell, Dubin, Gates, Black, Dershowitz, Branson[^15] Barr testified that he could not recall whether SDNY filed urgent reports beyond Epstein and Maxwell;[^16] he said a report "quite possibly" existed for Prince Andrew and that one should have been considered given the sensitivity.[^17] Barr testified it was possible that Geoff Berman's SDNY had not told him how deep it was in the investigation of particular individuals[^18] — Barr describes the SDNY as "relatively well-known for playing its cards very close to the vest."[^19]

## Witness Cooperation SDNY sought Prince Andrew as a witness;[^20] Barr testified that he was aware of a dispute over Andrew's cooperation.[^21] Geoffrey Berman made public remarks about the dispute outside Epstein's Manhattan residence on January 27, 2020, as reported at the time by the Associated Press[^29]; Barr criticized the handling.[^22]

## Post-Epstein Death

The investigation continued after Epstein's death, resulting in Maxwell's indictment.[^23] Whether any further investigation continued after Maxwell's conviction is unclear from Barr's testimony.[^24]

## Barr on the SDNY

- Barr argues SDNY's leak culture would prevent cover-ups;[^25] he also describes the SDNY as playing its cards very close to the vest[^26] and says it may not have fully briefed him.[^27]
- Barr never directly asked Berman which prominent figures were being investigated.[^28]

## Open Questions - Was the SDNY investigation the primary federal prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, as opposed to one of several concurrent federal proceedings? - Did the SDNY investigation run in parallel with the earlier Florida [Non-Prosecution Agreement (Florida NPA)](atlas-27a5255e75c8b7189218433d8640b0342bd1ed7114879ef40fa55ef4f56006a8.md), rather than only beginning after it concluded?

# MCC Death Investigation **Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.* Edition label: `2026-11` > Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Event:** Death of Jeffrey Epstein at Metropolitan Correctional Center (MCC), New York[^1] **Date:** August 10, 2019[^2] **Official ruling:** Suicide by hanging[^3] (Material Handler Thomas, who found him, described him suspended from the top bunk in a near-seated position)[^4] **Investigations:** The New York City Chief Medical Examiner ruled the death a suicide by hanging;[^5] the FBI found no criminality associated with the death;[^6] DOJ OIG found no evidence contradicting the FBI's determination.[^7]

## Timeline - **July 6, 2019:** Arrested;[^8] assigned to SHU[^9] (9 South, 9th floor)[^10] July 7 due to notoriety[^11] - **July 9:** Formal psychological assessment; denied suicidal history; no diagnosis[^12] - **July 23, 2019, 1:27 AM:** CO found Epstein with orange cloth around neck — cellmate said he tried to hang himself.[^13] Medical staff: friction marks on neck and knee.[^14] Placed on suicide watch.[^15] BOP administrative record: **Code 228 (SELF-MUTILATION)** disciplinary charge filed;[^16] Epstein placed in Administrative Detention July 29 pending DHO hearing.[^17] Charges ultimately NOT SUSTAINED (insufficient evidence).[^18] Epstein gave conflicting accounts: (1) cellmate tried to kill him; (2) he didn't know what happened; he later asked to be re-housed with the same cellmate.[^19] - **July 24:** Removed from suicide watch; placed on psychological observation[^20] - **July 30:** Psychological observation ended;[^21] **Psychology Dept emailed 70+ MCC staff** requiring Epstein be assigned appropriate cellmate.[^22] Warden selected new cellmate in consultation with BOP executive leadership; that cellmate remained until August 9.[^23] - **August 8:** USMS sent two emails to numerous MCC staff notifying them cellmate would transfer August 9 — no action taken.[^24] Epstein met with attorneys and signed new **Last Will and Testament** (MCC staff unaware until after death).[^25] - **August 9:** Cellmate transferred; no replacement assigned — in direct violation of the Psychology directive[^26] which supervisors told OIG they had communicated to all SHU staff, though several SHU staff said they did not know of it. Second Circuit unsealed ~2,000 pages of Maxwell civil documents;[^27] widespread media coverage.[^28] - **August 9 (6:58–7:19 p.m.):**[^29] Supervisor allowed Epstein to make **unrecorded, unmonitored phone call** in violation of BOP policy.[^30] Epstein said he was calling his mother; he actually called a personal contact.[^31] Identity not disclosed.[^32] - **4 PM, August 9:** The count was recorded inaccurately; staff did not physically count inmates.[^33] - **~8 PM, August 9:** All SHU inmates locked in cells; Epstein confirmed alone in cell.[^34] - **~10:40 PM, August 9:** Last observed approach to the L Tier before breakfast.[^35] No rounds or counts conducted after this time.[^36] **Count slips and round sheets were falsified** to show compliance.[^37] OIG found that an unnamed Material Handler worked 24 consecutive hours (3 shifts);[^38] the unnamed Material Handler told OIG that no one did the 10 p.m. count because they were tired.[^39] - **August 8, 2019:** DVR failure for most SHU cameras began July 29;[^40] MCC discovered on August 8 but did not repair before Epstein's death.[^41] - **August 10, ~6:30 AM:** CO Tova Noel and Material Handler Michael Thomas began breakfast delivery.[^42] Thomas found Epstein not responding — unlocked cell;[^43] found Epstein hanging from top of bunkbed with orange string, near-seated position, buttocks ~1–1.5 inches off floor.[^44] Thomas ripped string, lowered Epstein, performed CPR.[^45] Outside medical personnel arrived; Epstein transported to hospital and pronounced dead.[^46] - **August 10:** Barr recalled a morning call from his chief of staff, Brian Rabbitt, reporting an apparent suicide (Barr placed the call on a Sunday; August 10, 2019 was a Saturday).[^47] A supervisory staff attorney forwarded Warden N'Diaye's official notification at 1:57 p.m.[^48] - **August 10 (same day):** Barr directed IG Michael Horowitz to dispatch investigators;[^49] Barr later personally reviewed MCC security footage.[^50] - **August 11:** NYC Chief Medical Examiner autopsy:[^51] **cause — hanging; manner — suicide**.[^52] Toxicology negative.[^53] Multiple nooses were found in the cell on August 10.[^54] A family preservation request was sent to MCC seeking records held by the named agencies.[^55] - **Within one week:** Barr recalled replacing the BOP director and deputy within about a week[^56]; DOJ announced their appointments August 19, 2019.[^130] Barr recalled stopping MCC intake and believed he redirected prisoners to Brooklyn MDC; he did not date that action.[^57] - **August 27:** U.S. District Judge Richard M. Berman held a status hearing;[^58] defense asked the court to oversee the death investigation;[^59] the government opposed; victims spoke for 2.5 hours.[^60] - **June 2023:** DOJ OIG Report 23-085 published.[^61]

## Physical Evidence Supporting Suicide

From OIG Report 23-085 unless the item says otherwise; Barr's deposition overlaps on several points:[^138]

- Medical Examiner: injuries more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than a homicide by strangulation;[^62] no defensive wounds;[^63] no marks on hands; no broken fingernails; no debris under nails; no knuckle contusions; no body bruising (one arm abrasion consistent with convulsing from hanging)[^64]
- Toxicology negative for medications and illegal substances[^65]
- Prior incident July 23 (contested — Code 228 charges not sustained);[^66] placed on suicide watch[^67]
- Signed new Last Will and Testament August 8 (2 days before death)[^68]
- Unmonitored phone call to personal contact August 9[^69] (Barr recalled a call to someone he believed was a girlfriend in Byelorussia and interpreted it as consistent with saying goodbye[^70] — OIG: personal contact, identity not disclosed)[^71]
- Cellmate transferred; Epstein alone; excess linens including multiple nooses in cell[^72]
- Failed bail;[^73] Maxwell documents unsealed August 9[^74] with extensive media coverage[^75]
- Three interviewed inmates with sight of Epstein’s cell door told OIG nobody entered or exited that cell after his return.[^76]

## The "Perfect Storm of Screwups"

A phrase the questioner attributed to Barr, which he accepted, for six decisions or failures preceding or occurring that night:[^139]
1. Removed from suicide watch[^77]
2. No cellmate assigned[^78]
3. 30-minute checks not performed[^79]
4. Guards falsified logs[^80]
5. DVR not recording (see [DVR Failure (MCC Tier L Camera)](atlas-c6c36087a82eb0661e908f8fa2fb324a23b863415b576818a06c3bec3c3432d1.md))[^81]
6. Institutional counts not done[^82]

## Homicide Theory — Dr. Michael Baden

Medical examiner Dr. Michael Baden said the autopsy findings were more consistent with homicidal strangulation than hanging.[^129] Barr recalled no one expressing agreement with Baden during his conversations.[^83] OIG found nothing contradicting the FBI’s no-criminality finding; Barr was not aware of an investigation concluding homicide.[^84]

## Physical Access — SHU

Barr argued that undetected access up the stairway was not physically possible:[^85]

- SHU access requires remote central control door + key held by officers[^86]
- Two eyewitness inmates on the same tier saw no one enter[^87]
- "this would've required coordination from probably two dozen people maybe within the prison"[^88]

## FBI Independent Footage Review (July 2025)

The joint DOJ/FBI memorandum, labeled July 2025 in its PDF metadata,[^136] announced an independent FBI review of SHU footage:[^89]

- FBI enhanced the footage (contrast, color, sharpness) and posted raw and enhanced versions to the DOJ website.[^90]
- Confirmed: from ~10:40 PM August 9, 2019, to ~6:30 AM August 10, **"nobody entered any of the tiers in the SHU."**[^91]
- This claim is consistent with Barr's account but comes from FBI's own independent review, not Barr's briefing.[^92]
- The memorandum separately announces no further disclosure and cites footage in support of its suicide conclusion.[^93]

## Contested Footage

CBS reported the following observations from the released footage and its experts’ analysis:[^132]

- An "orange shape" on the stairs[^133]
- A possible third unidentified individual[^134]

Asked about the orange shape and a possible third person, Barr said he did not recall focusing on an orange shape[^94] and saw nothing of an unidentified person in the footage he reviewed.[^95] The camera directly covering Tier L was live-streaming but not recording due to [DVR Failure (MCC Tier L Camera)](atlas-c6c36087a82eb0661e908f8fa2fb324a23b863415b576818a06c3bec3c3432d1.md).[^96]

**Two additional cameras** (elevator bank,[^97] 10 South Officers' Station (adjacent unit; no view of the SHU)) were recording[^98].

## OIG Report Key Findings (23-085, June 2023)

The OIG identified numerous and serious failures, including:[^99]

1. **Cellmate requirement not met:** Psychology Dept's July 30 requirement[^100] was emailed to over 70 staff and, according to supervisors, communicated to SHU staff, though several SHU staff told OIG they did not know of it; USMS notified MCC August 8 the cellmate was leaving; no action.[^101]
2. **Records falsified:** Count slips and round sheets falsified.[^102] Multiple employees created false documentation;[^103] USAO SDNY declined prosecution of other employees for false records on the day before and the day of the death.[^104]
3. **Criminal prosecution → dismissal:** CO Tova Noel and Material Handler Michael Thomas charged federally for falsifying records — charges **dismissed** after successful deferred prosecution agreements.[^105]
4. **Camera failure:** DVR system failed July 29;[^106] MCC discovered August 8; not repaired before the death.[^107] FBI forensic analysis found 3 faulty hard drives; system never successfully reassembled.[^108]
5. **Staffing:** OIG found that an unnamed Material Handler worked 24 consecutive hours;[^109] the unnamed Material Handler told OIG the 10 p.m. count was skipped because they were tired.[^110]
6. **Cell security failure:** Excess linens in cell;[^111] records did not show when the cell was last searched;[^112] multiple nooses constructed and not discovered.[^113]

The OIG found **no evidence contradicting the FBI's determination** that no criminality was associated with the death.[^114]

## Aftermath Guards Tova Noel and Michael Thomas charged with falsifying records; charges dismissed via DPA.[^135] Other employees who falsified records on the day before and the day of the death were not prosecuted.[^115] Barr recalled being informed before action and said he was not involved in prosecutorial decisions.[^116] Barr recalled quickly reassigning the warden[^117]; the new BOP director was announced August 19, 2019.[^131] Eight OIG recommendations[^118] — all accepted by BOP.[^119]

## Open Questions

- Was DNA testing done on cell bedsheets?
- Which MCC recordings other than the released SHU common-area video remain unreleased, and what do the elevator-bank and 10 South Officers’ Station recordings show about activity elsewhere that night?[^123]
- Who did Epstein actually call on August 9 (OIG says personal contact, not his mother)?
- Do the IG and FBI reports fully reconcile the Baden hyoid findings?
- Was Epstein's body found in a ‘kneeling’ position, as a congressional questioner characterized the chief medical examiner's original finding, or in the near-seated position OIG and the Material Handler who found him described?
- Did Warden N'Diaye's August 10, 2019 death notification (forwarded by a supervisory staff attorney at 1:57 p.m.) reach Epstein's family directly, or only defense counsel and DOJ personnel?
- On what date did MCC New York actually stop new inmate intake and redirect admissions to Brooklyn MDC, given that Barr's recollection of this action was hedged and undated?
- How did the qualifications and shift assignments of the staff working in the SHU on August 9–10, 2019, affect their performance of required checks?
- Is the OIG report the most detailed primary source on Epstein's death?
- Was the July 29 DVR failure (one day before Epstein returned to SHU from psychological observation (BOP's SENTRY database wrongly recorded the return as July 29)) coincidental?
- Why were charges against other employees who falsified records on the day before and the day of Epstein’s death declined?

# Boland Amendment

**Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.*

Edition label: `2026-11`

> Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them.

**Definition:** A series of congressional restrictions on Contra aid (1982–1986), of which the committees designate the FY1983, FY1985 and FY1986 provisions Boland I, II and III,[^1] and the subject of a constitutional dispute between congressional authority and presidential foreign affairs power.[^2]

## Overview The "Boland Amendment" is not a single law but a series of restrictions sponsored by Representative Edward P. Boland (D-MA), Chairman of the House Intelligence Committee.[^3] The three restrictions are set out below.[^4] **Boland I** (December 1982, §793 of the FY1983 Defense Appropriations Act,[^5] Pub. L. 97-377):[^6] Barred the CIA and the Department of Defense from using the Act's funds to give military equipment, training, advice or other support to any group or individual not part of a country's armed forces "for the purpose of overthrowing the government of Nicaragua or provoking a military exchange between Nicaragua and Honduras."[^7] Limited in scope — it barred support given for the purpose of overthrowing the Nicaraguan government or provoking a Nicaragua–Honduras military exchange, and the Administration read it to turn on U.S. purpose rather than the Contras' intent.[^8] **FY1984 funding cap** (December 1983,[^9] Pub. L. 98-212[^10] and Pub. L. 98-215):[^11] Limited Contra support to $24 million for fiscal year 1984.[^12] **Boland II** (October 1984,[^13] §8066 of the FY1985 continuing appropriations act, Pub. L. 98-473):[^14] The operative version.[^15] Barred funds available to the CIA, the Department of Defense, or any other agency or entity "involved in intelligence activities" from being spent "for the purpose or which would have the effect of supporting, directly or indirectly, military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua by any nation, group, organization, movement, or individual."[^16] This remained in effect from October 1984 through December 1985.[^17] The Iran-Contra Committees found that both the letter and spirit of Boland II were violated.[^18] **Clark Amendment** (1976): An earlier statutory restriction on assistance for military or paramilitary operations in Angola[^19] — cited by the Minority as evidence that Congress knew how to restrict presidential covert action when it chose to (and that its failure to do so for NSC staff was intentional).[^20]

## The NSC Exclusion Dispute The Majority and Minority reports disagree on whether Boland II covered the National Security Council (NSC) staff:[^21][^25] **Majority position**: Boland II covered the NSC Staff.[^21] The catch-all phrase "any other agency or entity . . . involved in intelligence activities" was descriptive, not a term of art, and reached the NSC staff once it ran a covert operation.[^22] The Sciaroni opinion (by the counsel to the President's Intelligence Oversight Board, September 1985)[^23] finding otherwise was flawed — Sciaroni had never practiced law before becoming the Board's counsel, the opinion was his first on legislation, and it rested on the incorrect factual premise that the NSC was "a coordinating body with no operational role."[^24] **Minority position**: The NSC was **deliberately excluded** from the Intelligence Oversight Act of 1980[^25] (Harris's own 1980 proposal to include NSC was rejected during the drafting of the Intelligence Oversight Act).[^26] Draft C, an SSCI staff draft of a streamlined National Intelligence Act, would have confined special activities to the CIA unless the President determined that another agency should support an activity — it was not enacted.[^27] EO 12333 codified the NSC exclusion.[^28] The CIA legal memorandum distinguished participation, planning and providing advice for paramilitary operations (not permitted) from information-sharing, including advice on the delivery of supplies (permitted).[^29] The Minority argued that "virtually all, if not all, of Col. North's activities in support of the democratic resistance would have been legal even if the Boland Amendment had applied to the NSC."[^30] **Minority constitutional argument (Cheney et al.)**: Even if Boland textually covered the NSC, an appropriations restriction cannot abridge the President's Article II authority to conduct foreign policy.[^31] Where Congress cannot restrict a presidential action directly, the Minority argued, it cannot stop the President's staff from carrying it out; the Minority conceded that Congress could bar all U.S. Government spending on support for the Contras.[^32] This position — that even in Justice Jackson's "lowest ebb" category, whose framework the Supreme Court cited with approval in *Dames & Moore v. Regan*, 453 U.S. 654 (1981),[^33] Congress is "disabled" from interfering with some presidential foreign affairs matters[^34] — is an argument of the Cheney-led minority.

## Legislative History (Appendix A, William R. Harris)

The key primary source on the legislative history of the intelligence-oversight "entity" language is **Appendix A** of the Minority Report (Harris states that he does not know the specific legislative history of the Boland Amendments), authored by William R. Harris (longest continuously-serving SSCI consultant 1976–1984):[^35]

- NSC was **intentionally excluded** from IOA 1980 reporting requirements[^36]
- Harris's own 1980 proposal to include NSC was explicitly rejected[^37]
- Draft C (March 19, 1980) would have required special activities to be conducted only by the CIA, except when the President determined that another agency should support an activity — not enacted[^38]
- EO 12333 codified the NSC exclusion[^39]
- Harris's conclusion: presumption is NSC excluded, rebuttable by specific legislative history of particular Boland provisions — but the *default* is exclusion[^40]

## The Sciaroni Opinion

Intelligence Oversight Board counsel Bretton Sciaroni issued a September 1985 opinion finding Boland did not apply to the NSC.[^41] The Majority's criticisms of this opinion:[^42][^43]

- Had never practiced law before becoming the Board's counsel; the opinion was his first on legislation[^42]
- Rested on factual premises that turned out to be incorrect, including that the NSC was "a coordinating body with no operational role"[^43]

## The Diversion and Boland

The Majority argues the diversion itself violated Boland II and III because the proceeds came from selling United States weapons and so were United States funds.[^44] The CIA bought TOW missiles from the Department of Defense and delivered them to Iran through the Enterprise, acting as the CIA's agent.[^45] Because the proceeds were United States funds, the Majority found the diversion a violation of Boland II and III whatever the NSC's status.[^46]

## Open Questions - Did Congress legislate a resolution of the NSC-exclusion dispute after Iran-Contra, and how would that resolution apply to a later foreign-affairs funding restriction? - Has a federal court reached the merits of an appropriations-versus-Article-II dispute in a context that could bear by analogy on the Boland dispute? - Did the Boland Amendments as a whole bar U.S. government funds broadly for Contra support, and were the Iran-Contra operations as a whole, including the Iran arms sales, designed to circumvent them? - Given the Majority’s conclusion that the diversion violated Boland regardless of how narrowly the statute was construed,[^46] how did the Minority address the diversion separately from its NSC-exclusion argument? - Does the record itself characterize the Minority’s Article II/lowest-ebb argument as the core of its position? - Given the restrictions enacted through Pub. L. 98-215 and the Intelligence Authorization Act containing Boland III,[^11][^17] what distinct role did appropriations and authorization acts play across the Boland restrictions? - Given Harris’s account of the rejected 1980 NSC proposals and his rebuttable presumption for later Acts,[^37][^40] what specific legislative history would establish whether Boland II excluded the NSC?

# COINTELPRO

**Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.*

Edition label: `2026-11`

> Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them.

**Definition:** The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)'s Counter Intelligence Program (1956–1971) — a series of covert operations targeting domestic political organizations, using surveillance, infiltration, discrediting, and disruption tactics against domestic groups.[^1]

## Overview COINTELPRO ran from 1956 to 1971 under Director J. Edgar Hoover.[^2] It was not a single program but a series of named sub-programs targeting specific groups:[^3] - **COINTELPRO-CPUSA (1956)** — Communist Party USA[^4] - **COINTELPRO-SWP (1961)** — Socialist Workers Party[^5] - **COINTELPRO-White Hate Groups (1964)** — Ku Klux Klan (KKK) and white supremacist organizations[^6] - **COINTELPRO-Black Nationalist Hate Groups (1967)** — Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), Nation of Islam, Black Panther Party, and specifically Martin Luther King Jr.[^7] - **COINTELPRO-New Left (1968)** — Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), antiwar groups, campus organizations[^8] The program was exposed in 1971 after the FBI's resident agency in Media, Pennsylvania was broken into and the stolen documents were circulated and published by the press.[^9] Public exposure ended the formal program,[^10] but the Church Committee warned that COINTELPRO-type activities "may continue today under the rubric of 'investigation'" and found at least three post-1971 instances.[^11]

## Church Committee Findings The [Church Committee](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-94755-ii.pdf)'s Book II (*Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans*, 1976) sets out the Committee's findings on COINTELPRO; the detailed record is the COINTELPRO staff report in Book III.[^12] Key findings[^12]: **Tactics documented by the Church Committee (Book II and the Book III COINTELPRO staff report):**[^12] - Mailing anonymous letters to create suspicion between leaders and members[^13] - Sending anonymous letters to spouses to create marital problems[^14] - Notifying employers of political activities to cause job loss[^15] - Leaking derogatory information to "friendly" journalists[^16] - Obtaining targets' tax returns from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and trying to use IRS investigations or audits against individual targets (a protest leader; a professor)[^17] - Using informants to raise controversial issues at meetings to cause dissent[^18] - Falsely labeling group members as informants (the "snitch jacket"), which exposed them to expulsion or physical attack[^19] **Regarding Martin Luther King Jr. specifically:** - The FBI anonymously mailed King a surveillance tape and threatening letter that, his associates have said, he interpreted as an effort to induce him to commit suicide[^20] - The Church Committee found that the FBI tried to undermine ambassadorial receptions during King's Nobel trip and later efforts to honor him[^21] - On January 8, 1964, Assistant Director William C. Sullivan proposed that the FBI promote a new national civil-rights leader as King's successor once King had been discredited.[^22] Hoover approved exploring the plan, according to the Committee's staff report ([Book III](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-94755-iii.pdf)), which found it "uncertain whether the FBI took steps to implement Sullivan's plan"; the proposed successor told the Committee he was never contacted by the FBI[^23] **Lack of authorization:** The Church Committee found "no clear answer" to whether anyone outside the Bureau knew of COINTELPRO: the FBI produced documents showing that Attorneys General, presidential advisers, a House appropriations subcommittee and the Cabinet were put on notice of the CPUSA and White Hate programs, but none showing notice of the other three.[^24] The Committee judged many COINTELPRO proposals "clearly illegal", but the head of the FBI's Racial Intelligence Section testified that no one discussed the programs' legal authority: "No, we never gave it a thought."[^25] A 1974 Justice Department memorandum stated that COINTELPRO activities "may have violated" the civil rights, mail and wire fraud, and wiretap-disclosure statutes.[^26] **Concealment:** Internal FBI documents required that each operation "be designed to protect the Bureau's interest so that there is no possibility of embarrassment to the Bureau."[^27] The FBI kept records of some illegal techniques outside its normal files under a "DO NOT FILE" procedure, and at least one such memorandum was moved from Hoover's "Personal Files" to his "Official and Confidential" files shortly before his death.[^28] Carter administration charged Gray, Felt, and Edward S. Miller for illegal entries.[^29]

## Comparison with Hoover's Private Files

Where COINTELPRO used covert disruption against political organizations, Hoover kept some sensitive memoranda in his "Official and Confidential" and "Personal" files, and the Church Committee found that the widespread and accurate belief that the Bureau held derogatory information on politicians and critics created a "fear" of the Bureau.[^30]

heading_path: Relationship to Central Intelligence Agency Domestic Surveillance
text: ## Relationship to Central Intelligence Agency Domestic Surveillance COINTELPRO's FBI focus on domestic organizations ran parallel to Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)'s **Operation CHAOS** (1967–1974), which the Church Committee also documented: the CIA's Operation CHAOS, set up to find foreign links to racial, antiwar and other protest activity in the United States, which expanded its coverage of Americans; the staff report found that if the statutory ban on CIA 'internal security functions' is read broadly, CHAOS's basic mission violated the CIA's charter.[^31]

## Open Questions

- To what extent did COINTELPRO tactics continue after 1971 under different program names or informal authorization?
- Were any FBI officials prosecuted specifically for COINTELPRO activities?
- What Church Committee COINTELPRO materials remain classified?
- Which COINTELPRO and Operation CHAOS activities exceeded legal authority, and how did their authorizations differ?
- What was Frederick Schwarz's role in designing the Church Committee's COINTELPRO investigation?
- How do Book II's findings and Book III's staff report differ in their coverage of each COINTELPRO program's tactics?

## Related Entities - J. Edgar Hoover — Personally approved and supported each COINTELPRO program (per the Petersen committee, as reported by the Church Committee)[^32] - Frank Church — Chaired the Church Committee, whose Book II sets out its COINTELPRO findings - Frederick Schwarz — Church Committee general counsel

# Declassification Monopoly

**Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.*

Edition label: `2026-11`

> Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them.

**Definition:** This page's label for the asymmetry Olmsted (1996) describes: the executive branch's unilateral authority to declassify and disclose classified information for political advantage, together with its de facto power to characterize congressional disclosure as illegitimate "leaking".[^1]

## Overview The asymmetry has two components: 1. **Unilateral declassification:** Olmsted (1996) writes, "If the president wanted information disclosed, he could simply reveal it. The executive branch could declassify at will."[^2] (Olmsted 1996).[^3] 2. **De facto delegitimization of congressional disclosure:** When Congress publishes sensitive material — even material already widely reported in the press — the executive branch can characterize this as "leaking" or "endangering national security."[^4] Olmsted documents how Colby's November 1975 criticism of the Church Committee for publishing previously-reported names in its assassination report was used to imply the committee was endangering "human lives"[^5] — even though one of the named individuals had identified himself in a letter to the editor and Church Committee member Barry Goldwater (one of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)'s strongest supporters) agreed the names should be published.[^6] In Olmsted's account, the combination of these two — selective disclosure when it serves the executive's narrative, plus delegitimization of any congressional symmetric disclosure — produces an asymmetric information environment in which the executive branch can shape the public debate while constraining Congress's ability to rebut.[^7]

## Historical significance

In Olmsted's account, the president's monopoly on authorized disclosure was the most important weapon in the Ford White House's public-relations campaign, whose responses to the committees the [Intelligence Coordinating Group (ICG)](atlas-d151e008a67cac21e1402ad8a19dc3fbc25ff7f39c3c310975e615604d3afa41.md) coordinated:[^8]

- Cheney's December 27, 1974 advice to Ford, recorded in a draft memo (Olmsted) or meeting notes (Kitts), recommended a presidential "mechanism to investigate" whose goals included heading off "Congressional efforts to further encroach on the executive branch."[^9]
- The [Welch operation](atlas-66cdd8443ab6cb5a8313b378422f4b1137d81259c4061ec94a815378b253978d.md) (Dec 1975 – Jan 1976) drew on the executive branch's command of media attention: the White House staged the return and burial while leaving the blame for the killing implied rather than stated.[^10]
- The [Pike Report suppression](atlas-c3d52c8c6f8c310282d1e2a875c77e973f3b5d9dc42c95b0774b156429630a38.md) (January 1976) was driven by the executive branch's ability to reframe Pike's refusal to let the executive censor the final report as irresponsible "leaking"; in October 1975 Pike had accepted a procedure referring disputed disclosures to the President.[^11]
- Ford's Feb 1976 reform proposals included **criminal penalties for government employees' unauthorized disclosures of intelligence "sources and methods"** — including disclosures to journalists.[^12]

## Open Questions - How many previously public names did the Church Committee’s assassination report contain? - Has the Declassification Monopoly asymmetry been narrowed by statutory or executive-order changes since 2000? - Do the 2003 Plame episode, post-Snowden classification debates, or Trump-era disclosures exhibit the same disclosure asymmetry as the Ford-era episodes? - Beyond his membership in the Intelligence Coordinating Group and public criticism of the committees, did William Colby direct the executive branch’s use of its disclosure power?[^14][^15]

Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Definition (Barr's):** A compilation of people to whom Jeffrey Epstein made victims available — analogous to what a "bordello madam" would maintain[^1] **Status:** Barr was never told such a document existed[^2]

## Barr's Account William Barr was never briefed by SDNY that a "client list" existed as a discrete document or compilation.[^3] He was never briefed that SDNY had actionable evidence against any of the prominently named figures associated with Epstein.[^4] Barr did not proactively ask Geoff Berman whether any of these individuals were being investigated — he left investigators to follow the evidence.[^5]

## Maxwell Proffer: Named Clients (July 2025) Ghislaine Maxwell gave a list, from names she wrote down in advance of the proffer interview, of people she described as Epstein's clients:[^6] 1. **Leslie Wexner** (#1[^7] — "obviously there's the one very famous client that everybody talks about")[^8] 2. **Staley** (#2)[^9] 3. **Leon Black** (#3)[^10] 4. **Glenn Dubin**[^11] (Highbridge Capital — Maxwell said Epstein was heavily involved in its financing or sale to JPMorgan)[^12] Maxwell also mentioned a woman in Ohio whose name she couldn't recall.[^13] She explicitly states, "I was not part of Epstein's business world, except tangentially and obviously" — these are people she observed or heard Epstein discuss, not a comprehensive list.[^14] Maxwell listed four people she understood to be Epstein financial clients[^15] and said she was only tangentially involved in his business world.[^16]

## Hidden Camera Footage

Barr recalled that cameras were uncovered during searches of Epstein's Manhattan building, and thought also on the island and possibly at a New Mexico property; he said he had heard of these finds and could not remember whether this was during or after his tenure.[^17]

Barr never viewed the footage.[^18] Barr said he did not recall seeing evidence that Epstein used salacious material for extortion.[^19] Barr said in 2025 that he had no reason to think collected material was no longer in DOJ possession, but he had not reviewed it.[^20]

## Bondi Reversal (2025) Public statements about the client list that Senator Durbin characterized as contradictory:[^21] - **February 2025:** AG Bondi stated the client list was "sitting on my desk right now to review" (Fox News).[^39][^22] - **July 7, 2025 DOJ/FBI memo:**[^23] The memo stated: "This systematic review revealed no incriminating 'client list.'[^24] There was also no credible evidence found that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals as part of his actions.[^25] We did not uncover evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties."[^26] The July 7 memo preceded Blanche's July 24–25 proffer interviews of Maxwell by 17 days; any claimed causal relationship requires separate evidence.[^27] - **Les Wexner:** Described by HOGR Democrats as, “at one point,” Epstein's “only documented client.”[^28]

## Epstein's Own Emails

In emails released by HOGR Democrats,[^29] Epstein asserted that Trump knew about "the girls"[^30] and discussed potential leverage with Michael Wolff;[^31] the emails do not establish a client list or corroborate Epstein's assertions.

## Alfredo Rodriguez's Black Book (Filthy Rich) Rodriguez, Epstein's houseman,[^32] took the book from his former employer's residence[^33] and tried to sell information to Bradley Edwards, describing his compiled victim lists as "the Holy Grail or Golden Nugget."[^34] Rodriguez produced it during a November 3, 2009 meeting with an undercover FBI employee;[^35] Rodriguez was convicted of obstruction of justice.[^36] *Filthy Rich*, chapter 57, reports names including Donald Trump, Bill Clinton, Ehud Barak and Ralph Fiennes.[^37] Whether these names appear as victims, social contacts, or alleged participants is not established by the book.[^38]

## Open Questions

- Did SDNY compile any formal list of individuals investigated as potential co-conspirators?
- What does the hidden camera footage show?
- Were any urgent reports filed with Main Justice about prominent figures?
- What triggered the July 7, 2025 DOJ/FBI memo's reversal on Client List existence?
- What happened to Rodriguez's black book after he produced it to an undercover FBI employee in November 2009?
- Are the prominent names in Rodriguez's book the same individuals in the DOJ's hidden camera footage?
- What formal investigative status did SDNY assign to the prominent figures discussed in Barr’s testimony, beyond what Barr recalled being told?
- Is Rodriguez's book the clearest documented precursor to the "client list" question?
- Was the material Rodriguez withheld the most direct documented evidence of Epstein's network?

# Trafficking Victims Protection Act

**Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.*

Edition label: `2026-11`

> Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them.

**Definition:** The Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 (Pub. L. No. 106-386)[^13], as reauthorized and amended (including by the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008) — a U.S. federal statutory framework for criminal prosecution and civil liability for sex trafficking.[^14] The criminal and civil provisions discussed here include 18 U.S.C. §§ 1591 and 1595; the Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA) also includes provisions codified in Title 22; **18 U.S.C. § 1591** is the criminal Sex Trafficking offense[^1], and **18 U.S.C. § 1595** is the civil cause of action[^2].

## Overview

The TVPA's § 1591 establishes the federal Sex Trafficking offense;[^3] § 1595 creates a civil right of action for victims (and, importantly, for third-party "beneficiary" liability against persons or entities who knowingly benefited from participation in a venture they knew or should have known engaged in trafficking).[^4]

In the Epstein-network civil-liability record, Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA) claims are central to the major financial-institution cases: in *Government of the U.S. Virgin Islands v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.*, the Virgin Islands sought relief under § 1595(d) for alleged violations of § 1591(a)(2)[^5], while *Jane Doe v. Bank of America, N.A.*, invokes § 1595(a), including its should-have-known beneficiary liability[^6]. Judge Rakoff's May 2023 motion-to-dismiss opinion in the JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank cases analyzes the plaintiffs' claims that the banks knowingly benefited from participating in Epstein's Sex Trafficking venture under § 1591(a)(2) (participation, knowledge or reckless disregard that force, fraud or coercion would be used, and a benefit)[^7], and addresses the Virgin Islands' standing under § 1595(d).[^8]

# Arms-for-Hostages (Iran Initiative) **Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.* Edition label: `2026-11` > Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Definition:** The covert U.S.-Israel program (1985–1986) to sell arms to Iran in exchange for the release of American hostages held by Iranian-backed groups in Lebanon;[^1] Reagan publicly denied it was Arms-for-Hostages (Iran Initiative);[^2] Walsh's report concluded that Reagan "had convinced himself that he was not trading arms for hostages"[^3]

## Overview The Iran arms initiative began in the summer of 1985 with an Israeli proposal, brokered by David Kimche and mediated by Manucher Ghorbanifar, to sell U.S. weapons to Iran through Israeli intermediaries.[^4] The theory was that Iranian "moderates" could influence Lebanese hostage-takers to release American captives.[^5] Reagan authorized the initial Israeli sales without a written Finding[^6] — CIA General Counsel Stanley Sporkin drafted a retroactive Finding after the November 1985 HAWK shipment.[^7] The initiative ran from August 1985 to November 1986 — approximately 15 months of arms sales that produced limited hostage releases,[^8] generated $28.6 million in receipts from sales of U.S. government weapons to Iran for the Enterprise,[^9] and created the financial surplus that North and Hakim diverted to the Contras.[^10]

## Key Events **August 20, 1985**: Israel shipped 96 TOW missiles to Iran; first Israeli delivery.[^11] **September 14–15, 1985**: Israel shipped 408 more TOWs; 504 TOWs total.[^12] **September 15, 1985**: Reverend Benjamin Weir released — the first (and at this stage only) hostage freed.[^13] **November 1985 — HAWK fiasco**: 18 HAWK missiles shipped via CIA proprietary airline[^14]; Iranians rejected them — officials in Iran were upset that the wrong model of HAWKs had been delivered;[^15] Iran demanded return;[^16] CIA General Counsel Sporkin drafted a retroactive Finding.[^17] **December 5, 1985**: Reagan signed a Finding authorizing covert action; it explicitly described the operation as Arms-for-Hostages (Iran Initiative).[^18] Poindexter later destroyed this Finding[^19]. **January 7, 1986**: NSC meeting — Reagan, Bush, Shultz, Weinberger, Casey, Meese, Regan.[^20] Shultz and Weinberger opposed.[^21] Reagan approved continuation.[^22] The Finding explicitly instructed CIA not to brief Congress — which the committees' majority treated as a violation of the notification requirements (the minority called the withholding legal).[^23] **January 17, 1986**: New Finding signed — direct U.S. sale to Iran, with Israel no longer the seller (an Israeli charter still flew the missiles on the last leg).[^24] The Finding directed the CIA Director not to notify Congress, and the "gang of eight" (the leaders of each party in the House and Senate, and the Chairmen and Ranking Minority Members of the Intelligence Committees) was never notified.[^25] **From February 18, 1986**: Two shipments of 500 TOWs each, 1,000 total, were delivered to Iran —[^26] Southern Air Transport ferried the missiles from the United States to Israel, and an Israeli charter carried them on the last leg to Iran;[^27] Khashoggi fronted $10M through Lake Resources;[^28] no hostages were released.[^29] **April 1986 — Diversion Memorandum**: North's memo allocated $12 million of the residual funds from the planned arms transaction to the Contras — the "diversion"; the earlier $800K surplus came from the Israeli advance for the November 1985 HAWK shipment.[^30] **May 25, 1986 — Tehran Mission**: McFarlane-led delegation failed;[^31] Iran offered to release two hostages immediately and two more after the HAWK parts were delivered;[^32] McFarlane refused and departed.[^33] **July 26, 1986**: Father Lawrence Jenco released — partial gesture after the Tehran mission failure.[^34] **July 29, 1986**: Amiram Nir briefed VP Bush at the King David Hotel, Jerusalem, describing the initiative in detail.[^35] Craig Fuller took notes.[^36] **August 1986 — Second Channel**: Ghorbanifar replaced by "the Nephew"[^37]; at the October 6-8, 1986 meeting with the Second Channel in Frankfurt, Hakim continued the negotiations and worked out a nine-point proposal that went beyond the plan advanced by North.[^38] **November 3, 1986**: Lebanese magazine Al-Shiraa published story;[^39] Rafsanjani confirmed November 4.[^40] **November 13, 1986**: Reagan gave public speech denying Arms-for-Hostages (Iran Initiative) —[^41] Walsh later concluded that Reagan had convinced himself he was not trading arms for hostages.[^42] **November 25, 1986**: Meese announced diversion;[^43] Poindexter resigned;[^44] North fired.[^45]

## Walsh's Findings

The signed Finding explicitly characterized the initiative as Arms-for-Hostages (Iran Initiative), and the committees described arms transfers in exchange for hostage releases.[^46] Three hostages were released during the initiative (Weir, Jenco, Jacobsen); three more were taken (Cicippio, Reed, and Edward Tracy), netting zero improvement in the overall hostage situation.[^47]

## The Finding Problem

Reagan signed the January 17, 1986 Finding authorizing direct U.S. arms sales to Iran.[^48] The Finding explicitly instructed CIA not to brief Congress — which the committees' majority treated as a violation of the National Security Act's notification requirements (the minority called the withholding legal).[^49] The Finding directed the withholding of notice from the "gang of eight"; the committees' majority treated the withholding as a statutory violation, while the minority called it legal.[^50]

## Open Questions

- After the January 17, 1986 Finding directed the CIA not to notify Congress,[^25] was that direction ever rescinded, and if so when?
- What happened to the three additional American hostages taken during the initiative (Reed, Cicippio and Edward Tracy)? Were they eventually freed, and under what circumstances?
- Was the CIA proprietary airline that flew the November 1985 HAWK shipment St. Lucia Airways?
- Poindexter testified he destroyed the December 5, 1985 Finding because it was "politically embarrassing";[^51] did anyone else know of or authorize its destruction?
- Is the "Nephew"/"Relative" who replaced Ghorbanifar in August 1986 the same Ali Hashemi Bahramani named (with Kamal Darvish) in the January 21, 1987 Culvahouse PIOB submission?

# Maxwell's Whereabouts, July 2019 to July 2020 **Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.* Edition label: `2026-11` > Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Definition:** The interval between Jeffrey Epstein's July 6, 2019 SDNY arrest[^1] and Ghislaine Maxwell's July 2, 2020 FBI arrest in Bradford, NH.[^32][^2] In mid-August 2019, Maxwell's whereabouts were largely unknown to the public, the press, and (per public reporting at the time) federal authorities, although an FBI situation report dated Aug. 15, 2019 listed Maxwell as a co-conspirator.[^3] The In-N-Out Burger photograph dated Aug. 12, 2019 in Universal City, Los Angeles is a widely published alleged sighting of Maxwell during the period;[^4] the image's provenance and possible manipulation remain disputed.[^5]

## Overview After Epstein's death, press reporting suggested Maxwell could become a federal target.[^6] Per [NY Post](https://nypost.com/2019/08/15/jeffrey-epsteins-gal-pal-ghislaine-maxwell-spotted-at-in-n-out-burger-in-first-photos-since-his-death/) reporting published Aug. 15, 2019, AG William Barr stated on Aug 12, 2019: *"Any co-conspirators should not rest easy."*[^7] Maxwell had already left public view: the Post wrote that she "seemingly dropped from the face of the Earth when sex abuse allegations began to surface against her close pal," and the Daily Beast that she "vanished from public view after he was indicted";[^8] press speculation in the weeks after Epstein's death (Aug 10, 2019)[^9] placed her variously in the UK ("holed up in her British manor"),[^10] on the Massachusetts coast (Scott Borgerson's Manchester-by-the-Sea, MA mansion),[^11] or abroad ("Is she in Europe?").[^12] The In-N-Out Burger photograph dated Aug. 12, 2019 — published by the NY Post on Aug. 15 — is a widely published alleged sighting that punctuates this period, and its provenance is disputed (see below).[^13] Approximately 11 months later, on July 2, 2020, the FBI arrested Maxwell in Bradford, New Hampshire.[^33][^14]

## Evidence and Open Questions

The public record leaves several evidence questions open:

heading_path: Q1 — Provenance of the In-N-Out photo — DISPUTED
text: ### Q1 — Provenance of the In-N-Out photo — DISPUTED The [NY Post](https://nypost.com/2019/08/15/jeffrey-epsteins-gal-pal-ghislaine-maxwell-spotted-at-in-n-out-burger-in-first-photos-since-his-death/) originally framed the photograph as **"The Post found the socialite hiding in plain sight"** with a **"NO CREDIT"** photo annotation.[^15] The [Daily Beast](https://www.thedailybeast.com/photo-of-jeffrey-epstein-pal-ghislaine-maxwell-at-in-n-out-burger-was-staged-paper-claims/) later reported the Daily Mail's allegation that Leah Saffian staged the image, while [Frank Report](https://frankreport.com/2019/08/19/source-california-uk-attorney-took-pictures-of-ghislaine-maxwell-for-ny-post-and-attorneys-dog-in-photo-too/) quoted an unnamed source alleging that Saffian took and sold it to the Post; neither allegation has been independently established.[^16] **Reported indicators, which this page groups as one source cluster, plus a separate limited image analysis:**[^17][^18][^19][^20][^21] 1. **EXIF metadata** tagged **"Meadowgate"** — reported as matching a business associated with Saffian[^17] 2. **Dog identification:** The dog at Maxwell's feet is reported to be **Dexter**, Saffian's own dog, said to be prominently featured on Saffian's Facebook[^18] 3. **"Good Boys" billboard that Outfront Media's spokeswoman believed was Photoshopped:** **Outfront Media** (the outdoor-advertising agency that manages the bus shelter behind Maxwell in the photo) confirmed: *"We have no record of 'Good Boys' ever being posted"* at that location.[^19] The actual ad at that bus shelter since **July 28, 2019** was for **Providence St Joseph's Medical Centre**.[^20] 4. **Independent forensic analysis** by Adam Wandt (forensic photo expert, John Jay College of Criminal Justice) via Inside Edition: *"There's a wave of line going down her back that's indicative of Photoshop manipulation"* and *"There's also brush strokes visible at the bottom that would lead me to believe that somebody possibly added Miss Maxwell to this picture"*[^21] The photographer told the Post that Maxwell was dining alone; a published image shows two meals (one on the table and one on a bench below) and two phones.[^22] Published accounts offer competing, attributed provenance claims.[^38] The Daily Mail account, as summarized by the Daily Beast, alleged that Saffian staged the photograph; Frank Report quoted an unnamed source alleging that she took and sold it to the Post.[^23] The public record reviewed here does not independently establish those allegations or the Post's handler chain. The Daily Beast reported in August 2019 that Saffian could not be reached for comment; she later returned a call from LA Magazine but said "I don't give interviews," and the public record reviewed here does not contain a Saffian statement on the staging allegation.[^24] **Status:** Provenance remains unresolved. The Daily Beast, LA Magazine, and other stories repeat the Daily Mail allegation;[^25] [Inside Edition](https://www.insideedition.com/infamous-photos-ghislaine-maxwell-n-out-burger-show-signs-being-photoshopped-expert-says-55365) separately reports Adam Wandt's narrower opinion that somebody "possibly added" Maxwell to the image.[^26] The Daily Mail article was not directly available during review, leaving its underlying sourcing unverified.

heading_path: Q2 — Was the reappearance choreographed? — OPEN
text:
### Q2 — Was the reappearance choreographed? — OPEN

The available evidence does not establish that the reappearance was choreographed. Several outlets repeated a Daily Mail allegation that the appearance was staged; a separate expert said parts of the image may have been manipulated.[^27] Those reports do not establish who staged or supplied the image, and the public provenance remains unresolved. The questions below describe hypotheses, not findings.

- **Why this venue (Universal City In-N-Out), if the appearance was staged?** — possible answers include geographic accessibility from the Encino law office of Saffian, whose company Meadowgate Media Investments Inc the EXIF tag is reported to match[^28], tabloid-friendly visual aesthetic (fast-food incongruity for a British socialite), and the bus-shelter background that the alleged edit overwrote with the *Good Boys* ad[^29]
- **Why the *Good Boys* film as the alleged overlay?**
- **Why this timing — two days after Epstein's death + the same day as Barr's "Any co-conspirators should not rest easy" statement?**[^31]
- **How did the photograph reach the NY Post?** — the record does not establish who supplied it (the EXIF indicator is reported, not confirmed) or who at the Post handled it.

heading_path: Q3 — Where was Maxwell between August 2019 and July 2, 2020?
text: ### Q3 — Where was Maxwell between August 2019 and July 2, 2020? In its December 2020 bail application, the defense said Maxwell moved into the New Hampshire house in December 2019 and stayed there continuously for approximately seven months until her arrest.[^39] A guard, Martin Anthony Jackson, in an FBI report of his July 2, 2020 interview, said he arrived at the Bradford house on or about May 8, 2020, and that he was under the impression, from his conversations with Maxwell, that she had been there since before Christmas 2019 without interruption.[^40] The government's July 2020 detention memorandum alleged that she had been hiding in locations in New England and had moved locations at least twice; the Court's bail ruling on July 14, 2020 said she "moved to New England, changing locations on multiple occasions"; and the defense later answered that she was not "changing locations on multiple occasions".[^41][^63][^39] These accounts do not supply a complete itinerary for August to November 2019.[^39][^41] An FBI report of a July 13, 2020 interview gives the account of a witness who showed the property.[^71] The report says the buyers used the names "Steve Marshall" and "Jen Marshall", that the witness met them at the property on November 2, 2019 and again on or about November 5, 2019, and that they made an offer on or about November 6, 2019.[^71][^72] According to the report, the buyers said they were "currently staying in Ascutney, Vermont"; the woman using the name Jen Marshall said she was looking for a residence with "ultra privacy"; the witness said the buyers "needed to set up an LLC" and used "their own law firm in Boston"; the buyers indicated they "would be paying cash"; and at the December 13, 2019 closing "the buyers did not show up".[^72] The report says that after the arrest the witness saw photos of Maxwell in the papers and "recognized" Maxwell as the woman using the name Jen Marshall.[^71] This is one witness's account as the FBI recorded it.[^71] An email with a November 27, 2019 sender line of "Steve Marshal", spelled that way, says "our Boston law firm Nutter will execute closing documents on behalf of the LLC as the manager".[^73] In one released copy of the closing file, the bank's notice of the December 12, 2019 wire reads "ATTN: JEN MARSHALL" under "Originator to Beneficiary Information"; another released copy of the same notice has the name blacked out.[^74] The same report says the witness later identified the man who arrived first at the first showing as "Scott Burgerson", spelled that way, "from photos of same in the media".[^75] A note of a July 14, 2020 call with the FBI says agents showed the witness a photo of Borgerson.[^76] The two records differ on how the identification was made, and this page prefers neither.[^75][^76] Being at a viewing shows nothing about ownership or payment. The Bradford closing file names Granite Reality LLC, acting through its manager, as buyer and gives December 13, 2019 as the closing date.[^42] The file's recording sheet and a December 10, 2019 broker email give a price of $1,070,750, which the email describes as a reduction; a draft account summary in the government production gives $1,070,800, and an FBI affidavit, which spells the name Granite Realty LLC, gives $1,070,000; these figures differ and are not reconciled here.[^42][^43][^44] The closing ledger records a $994,279.12 wire from the LLC and a $100,000 deposit listed under the real-estate agency, and the wire notice names Citizens Bank as the sending bank.[^45] In July 2020 the government wrote: "It is unknown whether the defendant purchased the property in cash, or whether she has a wealthy patron who did so on her behalf".[^46] These closing records do not establish the ultimate personal source of the money or the LLC's beneficial owner.[^42][^45] New Hampshire's filings name three people as manager at different dates.[^77][^78][^80] A certificate of formation filed on November 18, 2019 and the 2020 annual report name Jeffrey W. Roberts, care of the Boston law firm Nutter McClennen & Fish LLP.[^77] A change filed on July 28, 2020, 26 days after the arrest, and the 2021 annual report name Leah Saffian.[^78] The state dissolved the company in September 2023 over unfiled annual reports or fees.[^79] A reinstatement and the annual reports for 2022, 2023 and 2024, all filed on September 16, 2024, name Scott Borgerson, so they do not show when he took over.[^80] He also signed the company's December 25, 2024 cancellation, which gives as its reason "House sold on 10/30/2024."[^81] These filings show who was listed as manager on those dates.[^77][^78][^80] They do not show why the manager changed, who owned or funded the company, or that any of these people knew of any conduct.[^77][^78][^80][^81] The draft account summary said the relationship between Maxwell and the Montpelier Trust "is unknown at this time" and inferred one, in part from the LLC's listed address, which it said matched the trust's apart from the ZIP code; it did not trace the house payment from the trust.[^43] A July 13, 2020 email from an FBI forensic accountant reported that the trust's account-opening documents listed Maxwell as grantor of an irrevocable trust established on July 31, 2018, and gave the trust's address of record at a Boston law firm, while calling its attached analysis a draft subject to change.[^47] An April 2022 government email in the released files includes a chart showing about $7.95 million moving on November 12, 2019 from "Montpelier Trust and Corporate Services, Ltd" to a brokerage account under Scott Borgerson's name, and $1.2 million moving from that account to Granite Reality on December 11, 2019, two days before the closing.[^82] The email says "proceeds actually flowed to it's purchase."[^82] The chart is a government summary, not a bank record: the email says it was derived from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, it carries a printed Bank Secrecy Act warning against further dissemination, and another released copy of the email has the chart blacked out.[^82][^83] We did not locate the underlying transactions for the chart's arrows, though our searches read text and could miss a scanned record. The chart's first box lists Ghislaine Maxwell as grantor.[^82] A grantor is not necessarily the owner of the money, and the chart does not show who beneficially owned the money or who owned the company.[^82] According to the FBI's report of the interview, the guard said a security organizer, Matthew Hellyer, had been retained by Maxwell's brother Kevin Maxwell to arrange former British Army members as security, and that the organizer paid him $350 per day; he also said Maxwell gave him a business debit card in the LLC's name for needed items.[^40] The report does not trace the organizer's funding or show that the debit card paid the guard's wages.[^40] The records do not establish who "Steve Marshall" was.[^76][^75][^84] According to a note of a July 14, 2020 call with the FBI, the United Kingdom phone number he gave came back to an individual whom a guard interviewed on the day of the arrest identified as someone who had previously worked as a guard for Maxwell; the note does not name that individual.[^76] The FBI's report of the witness interview, after recording the phone numbers the buyers gave, adds a database query identifying the user of a redacted cell phone as Marcus Wakefield.[^75] The numbers are redacted, so these records do not show whether that is the same number, or that he used the name.[^76][^75] The guard's interview report says that Wakefield provided security before him, and that before Wakefield "another person by the name of Steve (NFI) provided the security", NFI meaning no further information.[^84] The defense said Maxwell married her spouse in 2016, but that passage does not name the spouse or give an exact date.[^48] In a December 2020 bail opposition, prosecutors described Maxwell’s marriage and bank forms on which both spouses listed themselves as single.[^37]

heading_path: Q4 — What do the records show about pre-arrest contact, surrender and the arrest?
text: ### Q4 — What do the records show about pre-arrest contact, surrender and the arrest? Both sides' filings document pre-arrest contact between Maxwell's lawyers and federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York (SDNY).[^49][^50] The defense said its lawyers communicated with the government in July, August, September and October 2019 and in January and March 2020; the government said the two sides communicated on multiple occasions between July and October 2019 and briefly on two more occasions, most recently in March 2020.[^49][^50] At the July 14, 2020 bail hearing, defense counsel said they had been in contact "eight to ten times in the past year", all to urge the government not to bring the case, and the prosecutor said the communications had been "minimal" and had not included information about her whereabouts.[^64][^65] Both sides place a contact on July 7, 2019: the defense said Maxwell "reached out" through counsel the day after Epstein's arrest, and the government said counsel made contact when the FBI tried to serve her with a subpoena and could not locate her.[^51][^50] At the hearing the prosecutor instead said the communications began when the government "served" her with a grand jury subpoena; the two government accounts differ on service, and they are not reconciled here.[^65][^50] An FBI email dated October 8, 2019, with the subject "Epstein briefing", contains the line "Ghislaine Maxwell: Attorney proffer on 10/8/19", and gives no other detail about it.[^52] The parties dispute what that contact meant.[^53][^54][^50] In July 2020 the defense said that, had the government alerted counsel that she was about to be arrested, counsel would have arranged her "prompt, voluntary surrender".[^53] At the July 14 hearing the Court asked whether defense counsel had indicated to the government that, should there be an indictment, they were "seeking to arrange a voluntary surrender".[^66] Defense counsel answered that they were "urging them not to return an indictment and saying we were always available to speak", and, when the Court asked whether they were implying that they should be contacted for voluntary surrender, said "Yes, of course".[^66] The prosecutor later told the Court, "As defense counsel conceded, no offer along those lines was ever made", which is the government's characterization of that exchange.[^67] In December 2020 the defense said counsel would have provided her location had the government asked, and would have willingly arranged her self-surrender had the government reached out, and that counsel "were never given that chance".[^54] The government said that at no point did counsel disclose her location, offer to surrender her, or offer to bring her in to be interviewed, and it called the first two points "undisputed".[^50] These filings and the hearing state the dispute; they do not identify a specific surrender offer that the government accepted or refused.[^53][^54][^50][^66][^67] A July 1, 2020 FBI affidavit said the FBI did not know Maxwell's current location.[^55] A premises affidavit said a cell-site simulator found the target phone at the Bradford property at approximately 7:36 AM on July 2, 2020, and that cell site data placed the phone in and around Bradford for at least the past 30 days; those are statements about a phone, not a day-by-day account of her movements.[^56] The FBI's public-affairs bulletin that day reported the arrest at approximately 8:30 in the morning, labelling the time EST, and said she was taken into custody "without incident".[^57] Prosecutors alleged that agents announced themselves and directed her to open the door, that she ignored that direction and tried to flee to another room, and that agents breached the door.[^58] The defense said she moved to a safe room under a security protocol after a guard, assuming the agents were press, warned her by radio; the government answered that the agents announced themselves and wore clothing identifying them as FBI.[^59][^60] The bulletin's short description does not settle that disagreement and does not say whether terms had been discussed earlier.[^57] In its ruling at the July 14, 2020 hearing, which ordered her detained pending trial, the Court noted that she had stayed in contact with the government through counsel and that the government did not contest this, but said that staying in contact "means little if that was an effort to stave off indictment and she did not provide the government with her whereabouts", and that the circumstances of her arrest "may cast some doubt on the claim that she was not hiding from the government".[^68] The Court also said that even if she only wanted to hide from the press and public, "an assumption that the court does not share", her recent conduct "underscores her extraordinary capacity to evade detection".[^69] These are the Court's assessments in deciding bail, not findings of what happened before the arrest, and they do not settle the parties' dispute.[^68][^69] **Limit of the search:** A search on October 31, 2026 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA) and House Oversight Committee Production 01 held by this project read only the top-ranked results for each query, and a term scan covered the full text of the 2025 interview transcripts; these did not establish a 2019–20 surrender, immunity or safe-passage agreement with the Justice Department or the White House. **Limit of the hearing read:** The hearing transcript was located separately and is not part of that search; 59 of its 91 pages were read in full and the rest scanned by term, and it records the exchange above, not an identified surrender, immunity or safe-passage agreement.[^70] **Limit of these records:** Neither the arrest's outcome nor a limited search proves that negotiations did or did not occur. The July 24–25, 2025 interview of Maxwell by Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche and its written proffer agreement came five years after the arrest and are separate, later records.[^61][^62] Blanche said at the start of the interview, "I'm not promising to do anything", and the agreement says "THIS IS NOT A COOPERATION AGREEMENT".[^61][^62]

## Open Questions - **Question:** Which filed record names Maxwell’s spouse and gives the exact marriage date? **Consequence:** The bail passage in Q3 gives only the year 2016, so the page cannot date the marriage against the trust and property records. - On what date did Good Boys open in U.S. theaters, and what, if anything, would that establish about the date of the alleged image overlay? - **Question:** Who took the In-N-Out photograph, and what is the actual provenance chain that landed it at the NY Post? - **Question:** Where was Maxwell between August and November 2019, and which New England locations did the government mean? **Consequence:** Q3 has attributed accounts only from December 2019, so the first months of the period have no documented itinerary. - **Question:** What was said at the attorney proffer the FBI email records for October 8, 2019, and does any record outside the limited search in Q4 show surrender terms being discussed with the Justice Department or the White House? **Consequence:** Q4 documents contact and a dispute over surrender but not the content of any discussion, so the page can say neither that terms were discussed nor that they were not. - **Question:** Who are the members or beneficial owner of Granite Reality LLC, and who funded the company? **Consequence:** The closing records show a wire from the company and a deposit listed under the real-estate agency. Who funded the company is not established by any record we could confirm. The LLC's beneficial owner is not established. - **Question:** Why the on-the-nose reading material — Gup's CIA Book of Honor — in the disputed August 2019 photograph? - **Question:** What is the actual distance between Saffian's Encino law office and the Universal City In-N-Out, and does any source state it? - **Question:** What contemporaneous July 2020 reporting, if any, describes how long Maxwell had been staying at the Bradford, NH property before her arrest? - **Question:** Is there contemporaneous reporting establishing that Maxwell's whereabouts remained unknown to the public and the press across the entire interval between the two arrests, rather than only during the documented mid-August 2019 window? **Consequence:** Q4 records what the FBI swore on July 1, 2020 and the parties' accounts of counsel contact, but those do not measure what the public or the press knew. - **Question:** Was the Aug. 12, 2019 In-N-Out photograph in fact the only publicly circulated image of Maxwell during this period, or were there other published sightings the public record reviewed here has not surfaced? - **Question:** Did press and prosecutorial attention turn to Maxwell specifically, and before others in Epstein's circle, immediately after Epstein's July 6, 2019 arrest (rather than after his Aug. 10, 2019 death)? **Consequence:** Q4 records the parties' accounts of a July 7, 2019 contact and a subpoena, which do not settle comparative priority. - **Question:** Has the NY Post ever, at any point after Aug. 19, 2019, publicly addressed how the In-N-Out photograph reached it or whether it was altered before publication?

# Nes Ziyyona Facility

**Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.*

Edition label: `2026-11`

> Secondary-source summary. This page summarises published books and memoirs (Whitney Webb, Victor Ostrovsky, Gordon Thomas and Martin Dillon, Ari Ben-Menashe, Israel Shahak). Allegations are attributed to their authors and are not independently established by primary records held in this archive. Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them.

**Definition:** In Victor Ostrovsky’s 1994 memoir, a facility at Nes Ziyyona is alleged to have been used for prisoner detention, human weapons testing and killings.[^1] These claims are not independently established by custody, laboratory or investigative records here.[^1]

## Background

The Israel Institute for Biological Research (IIBR) states that it was established as a government research institute in 1952 at Ness Ziona, where it remains.[^2] Its official history describes biological and chemical research; it does not substantiate the memoir’s allegations of human experimentation.[^2]

## Ostrovsky’s account of 1968–69

Ostrovsky writes that, while a military-police officer in 1968–69, he transported prisoners to a holding facility in Nes Ziyyona.[^3] He attributes the human-testing account to a source;[^3] no custody or laboratory record independently corroborates it here. The following is Ostrovsky’s written narrative, not a direct quotation of that source:[^3]

Ostrovsky’s narrative alleges that Palestinian detainees were used to test whether weapons worked and how quickly they worked.[^4]

Ostrovsky reflects on his reaction in the same passage.[^5]

He writes that what frightens him in retrospect is “not the fact that it was taking place” but the calm with which he accepted it; this is his reflection on the account, not independent confirmation that testing occurred.[^6]

## The Soweto parallel Ostrovsky alleges that a source described testing of “new infectious diseases and new medication” for Israeli drug manufacturers at an outpatient clinic for Baragwanath Hospital in Soweto, and writes that a Baltimore hospital served as a Mossad cut-out.[^7] The account is a memoir allegation, not an independently verified clinic or medical record.[^7] For a related discussion of the memoir’s allegations concerning both locations, see Ostrovsky Nes Ziyyona Soweto Human Testing 1.[^8]

## The 1991 Madrid Bush-plot tie-back Ostrovsky alleges that three Palestinian detainees were to be framed in a plot against President George H.W. Bush in Madrid in 1991, and writes that he later heard from a source that the three, held in the Negev, were transferred to the Nes Ziyyona research facility and “terminated.”[^9] [Names withheld: alleged detainees.] Their identities and this account have not been independently corroborated here.[^9] The memoir returns to Nes Ziyyona in its account of the alleged Madrid plot.[^10] That narrative connection does not establish a continuing detention or killing program, nor independently corroborate the earlier human-testing allegation.[^10]

## Significance

The memoir links alleged episodes at Nes Ziyyona and Soweto;[^11] it does not independently establish a continuous institutional program. Custody, medical and investigative records would be needed to test these claims.[^11][^12]

Allegations in this memoir should not be used to corroborate one another without independent evidence.

## Connections - Ostrovsky Nes Ziyyona Soweto Human Testing 1 — related discussion of Ostrovsky’s Nes Ziyyona and Soweto allegations.[^13] - Ostrovsky Madrid Bush Assassination Plot 1 — 1991 Nes Ziyyona tie-back[^12] - [Ostrovsky, Victor. *The Other Side of Deception: A Rogue Agent Exposes the Mossad’s Secret Agenda*. First edition. New York: HarperCollins, 1994. ISBN 0-06-017635-0. Held electronic version.](https://archive.org/details/othersideofdecep00ostr) — source[^14] - Ostrovsky — memoirist who describes himself as a Giftlick military-police officer in 1968–69[^3]

## Open Questions

- What independently authenticated records, if any, could test the memoir’s allegation of human experimentation at Nes Ziyyona? The official history of the Israel Institute for Biological Research (IIBR) does not establish that allegation.[^15]
- If the prisoner transport occurred as Ostrovsky describes, are surviving military-police records available to test his account? The memoir supplies no such record.[^16]
- Can any independently authenticated custody or investigative record test the alleged 1991 transfer and killing of the three unnamed detainees? The memoir does not supply such a record.[^17]
- Are there independently reviewable records identifying the facility described in the memoir and testing any connection to IIBR? A shared place name does not establish institutional responsibility.[^18]
