# Iran-Contra Second Channel **Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.* Edition label: `2026-11` > Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Definition:** The Iranian-side intermediary relationship that replaced the discredited "First Channel" (Manucher Ghorbanifar) in August 1986[^1]; centered on a nephew of Iranian Speaker Hashemi Rafsanjani ("the Nephew")[^2]; active through the November 1986 exposure that ended the Iran arms initiative.[^3] Called "the Relative" in the Tower Board's and the congressional committees' narratives.[^4]

## Overview After Ghorbanifar failed multiple CIA polygraphs[^5] and the McFarlane–North May 1986 trip to Tehran ended without producing a hostage release[^6], North, Hakim, and Secord sought a new Iranian interlocutor with closer access to senior Iranian leadership.[^7] Rafsanjani's nephew became the principal Second Channel contact from August 1986.[^8] Hakim, who opened the channel, took part with Secord in the meetings with an Iranian emissary close to Rafsanjani from Brussels (August 1986) through Frankfurt and Mainz (October 1986)[^9]; in October North left Hakim to negotiate with the Iranians, and Hakim produced the nine-point plan.[^10] Two features of the Second Channel, compared with the Ghorbanifar relationship: 1. **Closer Iranian leadership access.** The Second Channel Iranians were viewed as more promising intermediaries for releasing the hostages, though the committees concluded they represented the same principals as the First Channel.[^21] 2. **Hakim's commitments beyond presidential policy.** Hakim extended North's earlier plan into the **nine-point proposal**, including a commitment to develop a plan to induce Kuwait to release the seventeen Da'wa prisoners (North's PROF-note version provides for "some," not all).[^11] The proposal went beyond stated U.S. policy[^12]; Poindexter testified that the President approved it, but Shultz testified that Reagan reacted with shock when told of it in December 1986, and Reagan then authorized Shultz to ignore "any unauthorized understandings"[^13]; [Walsh](https://archive.org/download/WalshReport/Walsh%20Report%20volume%201%20Investigations%20and%20Prosecutions.pdf) reported that North, Secord, and Hakim had worked out the formal plan, and that the Iranians later insisted on adhering to it with George Cave's apparent agreement.[^14]

## Significance and evidence The records this section cites: - [Walsh Vol. 1](https://archive.org/download/WalshReport/Walsh%20Report%20volume%201%20Investigations%20and%20Prosecutions.pdf) documents the negotiation history and the nine-point proposal.[^15] - Tower Report Part 3 funds-flow diagrams (Transaction 6, October 1986) attribute a $7M deposit into Lake Resources on September 26, 1986 to "Iranian representatives (the Second Channel)," with $2.037M transferred to a CIA Swiss account that had been closed[^16]; Walsh instead records a $3.6 million second-channel payment deposited on October 29, 1986 into the Enterprise's Hyde Park Square account.[^17] - [Iran-Contra Congressional Report 1987](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/SERIALSET-13810_00_00-002-0433-0000) narrates the Second Channel's role.[^18] - The Culvahouse PIOB Submission Folder 5 (January 21, 1987) contains a released two-name list giving Bahramani's and Darvish's names, filed in the folder assembled for submission to the President's Intelligence Oversight Board.[^19]

## Open Questions - Was the Second Channel a Rafsanjani-sanctioned strategic relationship for the Iranian leadership, or a factional intelligence-collection operation that the November 1986 Tehran leak ended? - Was the Second Channel emissary (“the Nephew” or “the Relative”) Ali Hashemi Bahramani, whose name appears in the Culvahouse two-name list?[^19] - What role, if any, did Kamal Darvish, named in the Culvahouse two-name list,[^19] play in the Second Channel? - Was the two-name list in the Culvahouse submission intended to identify the Second Channel emissary and his associates? - How did the Second Channel’s September and October 1986 payments relate to the diversion of arms-sale proceeds? - Given the disputed testimony about presidential approval[^13] and Reagan’s later authorization for Shultz to ignore “any unauthorized understandings,”[^20] what commitments under Hakim’s nine-point proposal, including the Da’wa proposal, remained operative after the November 1986 exposure?

## Related Entities - Ali Hashemi Bahramani — Named in the Culvahouse submission - Kamal Darvish — co-listed in the PIOB submission - Hashemi Rafsanjani — Iranian Speaker - Manucher Ghorbanifar — predecessor First Channel - Oliver North — primary U.S. counterpart - Albert Hakim — Enterprise financial officer; nine-point-proposal negotiator - Richard Secord — Enterprise principal

# Suicide Watch Protocols **Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.* Edition label: `2026-11` > Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them. **Context:** Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) protocols for monitoring high-risk detainees at Metropolitan Correctional Center (MCC)[^1] **Relevance:** Multiple simultaneous protocol failures directly preceded Jeffrey Epstein's death[^2]

## Standard Protocol

The OIG report describes distinct requirements rather than one universal suicide-watch protocol: suicide watch involved direct continuous observation[^3]; twice-hourly rounds and institutional counts were general SHU duties[^4]; and the post-observation cellmate direction named Epstein, although an MCC New York local policy also required that inmates discharged from suicide watch be assigned a cellmate:[^5]

- Continuous or frequent observation (step-down levels)[^6]
- Cellmate assignment when removed from formal suicide watch[^7]
- Documented SHU rounds at least twice each hour, once in each half-hour, on an irregular schedule no more than 40 minutes apart[^8]
- Institutional population counts[^9]

## Failures in Epstein Case The following failures were all in effect on the night of August 9–10, 2019, though their onset was staggered over the preceding weeks:[^10] 1. **Removed from suicide watch** — after the unresolved July 23 incident, which officials treated as a possible suicide attempt, Epstein was stepped down from formal suicide watch[^11] 2. **No cellmate assigned** — a written July 30 Psychology Department direction required Epstein to have an appropriate cellmate after observation ended[^12]; no replacement cellmate was assigned after his cellmate was transferred out on August 9[^13] 3. **Required SHU rounds not performed** — Tova Noel and Michael Thomas failed to conduct checks[^14] 4. **Falsified logs** — OIG found that both guards falsified records to indicate checks had been made[^15] 5. **DVR not recording** — see [DVR Failure (MCC Tier L Camera)](atlas-c6c36087a82eb0661e908f8fa2fb324a23b863415b576818a06c3bec3c3432d1.md); the camera covering his tier was live but not recording[^16] 6. **Institutional counts not done** — the regular institutional headcount was not performed[^17] William Barr described this as "a perfect storm of screwups"[^18]. On the missed checks, he said it was apparently a consistent practice; the OIG reported finding no evidence contradicting the FBI's determination of no criminality in how Epstein died.[^19]

## Institutional Response Barr described his response to the death as follows:[^20] - Appointed a new BOP Director and Deputy Director, Kathy Hawk Sawyer and Tom Kane[^27][^21][^23] - Reassigned the MCC warden[^22] Barr also recalled stopping new intake to MCC and believed he redirected it to Brooklyn MDC; he did not date that action.[^24] Guards Noel and Thomas were indicted for falsifying records[^25]; both entered deferred prosecution agreements, and the charges were dismissed after they fulfilled the agreements[^26]. # Intelligence Budget Secrecy

**Reference.** *Reports what the sources say. States no conclusion of ours.*

Edition label: `2026-11`

> Not everything on this page is footnoted. Our citation check covers the main text, but not headings, the lists of related entries and sources, or open questions, which may state facts without a footnote. Check the footnoted text or the source before relying on them.

**Definition:** The systematic concealment of true intelligence expenditure from Congress through misrepresentation, omission, reclassification, and organizational fragmentation.[^1] The Pike Committee found, for example, that the first total of federal domestic-intelligence costs, compiled by the Office of Management and Budget at the Committee's request, was "more than five times" the amount given to the Committee in testimony.[^2]

## Overview

Its findings documented multiple distinct methods by which intelligence expenditure was kept out of the official totals, so that neither Congress nor government auditors could determine actual intelligence expenditure.[^3]

The Pike Committee found that there was no single budget figure that captured total intelligence spending, and suggested this may have been deliberate.[^4] Multiple agencies applied their own budget standards with no central authority capable of enforcing consistent definitions.[^5] As the Director of Central Intelligence acknowledged, there was no agreed definition of "intelligence" within the government.[^6]

## Concealment Techniques Documented

**Stated vs. actual totals.** GAO accountants on loan to the Pike Committee concluded that the foreign-intelligence budget was three to four times more costly than Congress had been told.[^7] An OMB review of the domestic intelligence budget, conducted at the committee's request, found costs may be 5x higher than stated.[^8] A 1971 Schlesinger/OMB study concluded the foreign intelligence budget was "nearly double the amount being told to Congress."[^9]

**NSA omission.** The National Security Agency (NSA) — which did "nothing else except gather and analyze technical intelligence" — had roughly 20 percent of its budget excluded from the intelligence aggregate presented to Congress.[^10]

**Transfer and reclassification.** DoD transferred items from the intelligence budget to "Communications," "Research and Development," and other categories, shifting hundreds of millions of dollars and thousands of personnel.[^11] The Advance Location Strike Program, Mapping/Charting/Geodesy, and Counterintelligence and Investigative Activities were all reclassified.[^12] Entire agencies (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) were omitted from intelligence-related cost estimates.[^13]

**Undervaluation.** In one covert operation the Committee analyzed, CIA valued the weapons supplied at about half their Defense Department contract prices.[^14] Submarine repair costs and military base support for intelligence operations were not allocated to intelligence budgets under any consistent standard, and some intelligence activities were reclassified as research and development.[^15]

**Reprogramming without approval.** CIA's budget appeared as a single line item in the published federal budget ("secrecy").[^16] CIA could then tell Congress it was spending a certain amount on covert action, then "proceed to transfer large amounts to covert programs without Congress' approval."[^17] This gave CIA "an unusual advantage" over other agencies subject to congressional reprogramming restrictions.[^18]

**Agency fragmentation.** The Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) presented the entire foreign intelligence budget but had authority only over CIA's budget; Defense officials testified that a "substantial part" of their intelligence budget was the responsibility of the Secretary of Defense, and that the DCI "merely reviews their work."[^19] FBI did not know whether CIA had a counterintelligence group, how much CIA's operations cost, or whether CIA duplicated FBI work.[^20]

## GAO Exclusion

The Pike Report states that from 1962 the General Accounting Office (renamed the Government Accountability Office in 2004)[^33], Congress's auditor, made no attempt to audit the CIA because it was allowed only "scant access" to classified spending.[^21] According to the Pike Report, when GAO was directed to compile basic budgetary information on federal investigative and intelligence functions, it was refused information by CIA, NSA and Defense Department intelligence agencies; GAO's own letter in the hearing record says the request came from the Senate Government Operations and Senate Budget Committees and that OMB refused the data for CIA, NSA and certain other sensitive Defense intelligence activities.[^22] The FBI allowed GAO to examine summaries but refused to permit verification of those summaries.[^23]

Paradoxically, the CIA gave a private consulting firm (Peat Marwick Livingston & Co.) full access to all classified procurement documents and personnel in 1966.[^24] CIA could have saved money by giving GAO that same access; instead it hired the private firm for $55,725.[^25]

## CIA Internal Audit Failures

CIA's own audit staff was undermanned for a comprehensive review of the agency's worldwide spending.[^26] Only 5% of vouchered transactions were checked, even though these represented 20% of CIA's entire budget.[^27] Auditors were not always allowed to know the exact purpose of expenditures.[^28] Auditor recommendations were "usually not disclosed" in the auditor's report to headquarters.[^29] Overseas stations were not audited on a regular basis; it could be two or three years, or more, before a station was audited.[^30] The CIA's own internal standards deviated from Certified Public Accountant standards, and no list of permitted deviations was maintained.[^31]

## Policy Significance

The Pike Report found that keeping the intelligence budget total secret was in "direct conflict" with the U.S. Constitution's requirement to publish "a [regular] Statement and Account of the Receipts and Expenditures of all public Money" (Art. I, Sec. 9).[^32]

## Open Questions - How does the scope of the Pike Committee’s public accounting of budget concealment compare with other congressional investigations? - Without accurate expenditure information, how far can congressional oversight committees enforce statutory limits on intelligence spending? - What authority did Henry Kissinger hold over Covert Action budgets through the Forty Committee or otherwise? - Was [Covert Action](atlas-20f37534162bdbffa86714d1f40ef633eb5f92724321bbf4b7abb6d8cedc208a.md) the largest single category of concealed intelligence spending? - Does budget secrecy let the executive set the terms on which Congress negotiates [oversight](atlas-d96435dc573bddd66705ad8a23737720bc56d00efe328b69dc6c92ab517eac65.md)? - What is the current ratio of stated to actual intelligence expenditure? - Did any later statute require public disclosure of an intelligence budget total, and if so, does that total still omit spending of the kind the Pike Report described, such as the roughly 20 percent of NSA's budget left out of the intelligence total[^10]?
